summary: Describes a flexible way to represent time values, such as an interval or a duration, in the generalized MANET packet and message format. It defines Message and Address Block TLVs for validity and interval times.

plainLanguage.summary:
A routing protocol for a wireless network where the devices move around needs to tell other devices when to expect its next message and when the information it sent has gone stale.

This document gives those times a compact encoding, so that a time takes one byte and can still cover anything from a fraction of a second to several weeks. The encoding can also depend on how many hops away the reader is, so the same message asks for different behaviour near the sender and far from it.

subtitle: A compact way for ad hoc network protocols to say how often to expect a message and how long its contents stay valid.

tldr.problem: Routing protocols for mobile ad hoc networks need to say two things about their messages: how soon the next one of the same kind should arrive, and how long the information in this one stays true. Carrying those times in full takes too many bytes on a bandwidth-limited wireless link.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Time TLV whose value is an 8-bit time-code, formed from a 5-bit exponent and a 3-bit mantissa, scaled by a parameter C that every node in the deployment shares. The TLV can also carry a list of time codes with the hop count at which each takes effect, so a node works out its own value from how far away the originator is.
tldr.outcome: A time value can range from C up to 15 * 2^28 * C, which is about 45 days when C is 1/1024 of a second, using one byte. Two Message TLV types, INTERVAL_TIME and VALIDITY_TIME, and two matching Address Block TLV types are defined for use with the generalized MANET packet format.

facts.label: Hop count when it is not known

today: RFC 5497 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It defines the INTERVAL_TIME and VALIDITY_TIME TLV types in the Message and Address Block TLV registries of RFC 5444, and it depends on that generalized MANET packet and message format.

sections.title: What This Document Adds
sections.content:
The generalized packet and message format of RFC 5444 specifies a signaling format that MANET routing protocols can employ for exchanging protocol information. That format can express and associate attributes to packets, messages or addresses by way of a general TLV, type-length-value, mechanism.

This document specifies a general Time TLV structure that any MANET routing protocol can use when it needs to express either single time-values or a set of time-values with each time-value associated with a range of hop counts, as provided by the Message Header of RFC 5444. This allows a receiving node to determine a single time-value if it either knows its hop count from the originator node or the Time TLV specifies a single time-value.

A time-value is, in this context, not an absolute point in time, but an interval or a duration. An instance of a Time TLV can express an interval or a duration such as 10 seconds.

The document also specifies two Message TLV Types that use the proposed structure. These are INTERVAL_TIME and VALIDITY_TIME, specifying respectively the maximum time before another message of the same type as this message from the same originator should be received, and the duration for which the information in this message is valid after receipt. If both are present, the latter will usually be greater than the former, in order to allow for possible message loss.

Two Address Block TLV Types are specified as well, again INTERVAL_TIME and VALIDITY_TIME, defined equivalently to the two Message TLVs with the same names.
sections.plainLanguage: The MANET packet format of RFC 5444 lets a protocol attach small pieces of extra information to a packet, a message or a list of addresses. This document defines one such piece: a way of saying how long a time is.

sections.title: Why Time Needs Its Own Encoding
sections.content:
The Time TLV structure is intended to be used as a component in a MANET routing protocol, for example to indicate the expected spacing between successive transmissions of a given Message Type, by including a Time TLV in transmitted messages.

Some MANET routing protocols use very short spacing for some messages and very long spacing for others, or change the message transmission rate according to observed behaviour. If a network is observed at some point to exhibit a highly dynamic topology, a sub-second message spacing could be appropriate, whereas if the network later stabilises, multi-hour spacing may become appropriate. Different MANET routing protocols and different deployments may have different granularity requirements and bounds on the shortest and longest spacing between successive message transmissions.

MANET routing protocol deployments also typically use bandwidth-limited wireless network interfaces, and therefore prefer to trade off computational complexity for a saving in the number of bits transmitted. That is practical here, because the intended uses of Time TLVs, including message interval time and information validity time, do not require high-precision values of time.

The structure caters to these characteristics by encoding time-values, such as an interval or a duration, in an 8-bit field; by allowing these time-values to range from very small, for example 1/1024 second, to very long, for example 45 days; and by allowing a routing protocol or a deployment to parameterize this, to attain finer granularity at the expense of a lower upper bound, through a single parameter, C. The parameter C must be the same for all MANET routers in the same deployment.

The TLV mechanism of RFC 5444 allows associating a value to a packet, a message or addresses. The data structure is identical in all three cases, but the TLV's position in a received packet determines what it is: a Packet TLV appears in the Packet Header before any messages, a Message TLV appears in the TLV Block immediately following a Message Header, and an Address Block TLV appears in the TLV Block immediately following an Address Block. While TLVs may be structurally identical, what they express may be different, which is why RFC 5444 specifies separate registries for Packet TLV Types, Message TLV Types and Address Block TLV Types.
sections.plainLanguage: Two forces shape this design. Wireless links in these networks carry few bits, so a time should not cost many bytes. And the times a routing protocol cares about do not need to be precise, because they describe how long to wait and how long to trust something, not an exact instant.

sections.title: Encoding a Time Value in 8 Bits
sections.content:
Time-values are each represented in an 8-bit time-code, one or more of which may be used in a TLV's value field. Of these 8 bits, the least significant 3 bits represent the mantissa, a, and the most significant 5 bits represent the exponent, b, so that the time-value is (1 + a/8) * 2^b * C and the time-code is 8 * b + a.

All nodes in the MANET MUST use the same value of the constant C, which is specified in seconds, so all time-values are in seconds too. C MUST be greater than 0 seconds. Ascending values of the time-code represent ascending time-values, so time-values may be compared by comparing time-codes.

An algorithm for computing the time-code representing the smallest representable time-value not less than a given time-value t is given in the RFC: find the largest integer b such that t/C is at least 2^b; set a to 8 times (t divided by C times 2^b, minus 1), rounded up to the nearest integer; if a equals 8, set b to b plus 1 and set a to 0; and then, if a is between 0 and 7 and b is between 0 and 31, the required time-value can be represented by the time-code 8 * b + a, otherwise it cannot.

The minimum time-value that can be represented is C. The maximum is 15 * 2^28 * C, or about 4.0 * 10^9 * C; if C is 1/1024 second, that is about 45 days. A protocol using this time representation MUST define the value of C, and MAY specify that the all-bits zero time-value represents a time-value of zero and/or that the all-bits one time-value represents an indefinitely large time-value.
sections.plainLanguage:
The encoding works like a rounding scheme. Five bits hold a power of two and three bits hold a fraction of it, so the byte can stand for a wide range of durations while still ordering correctly: a bigger number always means a longer time.

One number, C, is shared by everyone in the network. It sets the unit. Choosing C as a thousandth of a second gives times from a thousandth of a second up to about 45 days.

sections.title: The Time TLV Structure
sections.content:
The data structure allows the representation of a single time-value, or of a default time-value plus pairs of time-values and hop counts for when hop-count-dependent time-values are required. Using the regular expression syntax of RFC 5444, it is specified as <time-data> = (<time-code><hop-count>)*<time-code>.

A time-code is an 8-bit unsigned integer field containing a time-code, and a hop-count is an 8-bit unsigned integer field specifying a hop count from the message originator. A time-data structure therefore consists of an odd number of octets: with a repetition factor of n for the (time, hop count) pairs, it contains 2n+1 octets, and on reception n is determined from the length.

The structure may be written as <t_1><d_1><t_2><d_2> ... <t_n><d_n><t_default>. The hop counts d_1 to d_n, if present, MUST be a strictly increasing sequence with d_n less than 255. At the receiving node's hop count from the originator, the indicated time-value is t_1 if n is greater than 0 and the hop count is at most d_1; t_i+1 if n is greater than 1 and d_i is less than the hop count and at most d_i+1; and t_default otherwise, that is, if n is 0 or the hop count is greater than d_n.

Two variants of the TLV exist. A single-value Time TLV, with the tismultivalue flag cleared in its tlv-flags field, contains a single time-data structure in its value field, and its length field MUST contain the value 2n+1, with n being the number of (time-value, hop count) pairs. The number of pairs is found from the length as n := (length - 1) / 2, and that MUST be an integer value.

A multi-value Time TLV, with the tismultivalue flag set, contains a sequence of time-data structures, associating a set of them with an identically sized set of addresses. Multi-value Time TLVs MUST be Address Block TLVs, and MUST NOT be a Packet TLV or a Message TLV. Their length field MUST contain the value m * (2n+1), where n is the number of (time-value, hop count) pairs and m is the number of values as defined in RFC 5444. The number of pairs in each time-data structure is found as n := ((length / number-values) - 1) / 2, and that MUST be an integer value; the lists of hop count values MAY be different.

Hop count is defined as the number of hops from the message originator to the message recipient, equal to the msg-hop-count field in the msg-header element of RFC 5444 if present, after it has been incremented on reception. If that field is not present, or in a Packet TLV, hop count is defined to equal 255. A time-data structure included in a message without a msg-hop-count field, or in a Packet TLV, SHOULD use the single time-code form, that is, n = 0.
sections.plainLanguage: The value of the TLV is a list of time codes, each optionally followed by the hop count at which it starts to apply. A node that knows how many hops away it is looks up the entry that covers its own hop count, and uses that time. Everything beyond the last hop count uses the final, default entry.

sections.title: The Message TLVs and the Address Block TLVs
sections.content:
Two Message TLVs are defined, for signalling message interval and message validity time.

An INTERVAL_TIME Message TLV defines the maximum time before another message of the same type as this message from the same originator should be received. This interval time MAY be specified to depend on the hop count from the originator, which is appropriate if messages are sent with different hop limits so that receiving nodes at greater hop counts have an increased interval time. A message MUST NOT include more than one INTERVAL_TIME TLV.

A VALIDITY_TIME Message TLV defines the validity time of the information carried in the message in which the TLV is contained. After this time the receiving node MUST consider the message content to no longer be valid, unless it is repeated in a later message. The validity time of a message MAY also be specified to depend on the hop count from its originator, which is appropriate if messages are sent with different hop limits so that receiving nodes at greater hop counts receive information less frequently and must treat it as valid for longer. A message MUST NOT include more than one VALIDITY_TIME TLV.

Two Address Block TLVs are defined with the same names. An Address Block INTERVAL_TIME TLV defines the maximum time before this address from the same originator should be received again, and its interval time MAY depend on the hop count from the originator. An Address Block VALIDITY_TIME TLV defines the validity time of the addresses the TLV is associated with; after this time the receiving node MUST consider the addresses to no longer be valid, unless they are repeated in a later message, and the validity time MAY depend on the hop count.

A protocol that uses an Address Block TLV and the same named Message TLV MUST specify how to interpret the case when both are present, typically that the former overrides the latter for the addresses it covers.

In the terminology of the document, a time-value is a time measured in seconds and a time-code is the 8-bit field that represents a time-value.
sections.plainLanguage:
Two questions are answered by the TLVs. The interval TLV says how long the sender intends to wait before sending the same kind of message again, so a receiver knows when to expect it. The validity TLV says how long the contents should be trusted after they arrive.

Both can be attached to a whole message or to a list of addresses inside a message, and both can say that the time grows with distance from the sender.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
This specification defines two Message TLV Types, allocated from the Assigned Message TLV Types repository of RFC 5444, and two Address Block TLV Types, allocated from the Assigned Address Block TLV Types repository of RFC 5444. IANA has assigned the same numerical value to the Message TLV Type and the Address Block TLV Type with the same name.

INTERVAL_TIME is assigned type 0 and VALIDITY_TIME is assigned type 1 in both registries, with type extension 0. Type extensions 1 to 223 require Expert Review and 224 to 255 are for Experimental Use.
sections.plainLanguage: The two new TLVs are registered in the registries of RFC 5444, and the message version and the address list version share the same numbers: zero for the interval and one for the validity time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document specifies how to add data structures, TLVs, that provide timing information to packets and messages specified using RFC 5444. In particular, information validity durations and reporting intervals may be added.

The general security threats that apply are those general to RFC 5444, problems of integrity and confidentiality. With regard to integrity, modification of a Time TLV can cause information to have an invalid validity time or expected interval time, which may cause incorrect protocol performance. Modification or addition of timed information can add to a protocol's workload, especially if a short validity time is specified, and to its storage requirements, especially if a long validity time is specified.

To counter these threats, the security suggestions in RFC 5444 for the use of authentication and encryption are appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: The times inside these TLVs are only as trustworthy as the message carrying them. An attacker who changes a validity time can make the network do more work or trust stale information for longer, so the same authentication and encryption used for the rest of the message are the right protection.

fields.name: Exponent b
fields.desc: The most significant 5 bits. The time-value is (1 + a/8) * 2^b * C.

fields.name: Mantissa a
fields.desc: The least significant 3 bits. The time-code is 8 * b + a.
